items.mnemonic_text: A wagon (軍) moving down a road (辶): to carry, one's fortune.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, someone straps a tarp <radical>cover</radical> over the little <radical>vehicle</radical> — axle, two wheels — so nothing spills. They plant footstep after footstep to <radical>advance</radical> it up the steep climb toward the vending machine at the top. Whatever survives the grind has been carried — and arriving at all on a slope like that counts as pure <kanji>luck</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up, the hiker hauling the cart — everyone just calls her <reading>Oona</reading> — grunts <reading>うん</reading> with every step, the same sound as her own name. At the top, the vending machine rewards her stubbornness with a drink that isn't even the one she wanted.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝公園で運動する。
example_sentences.english: I exercise in the park every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]公[こう]園[えん]で運[うん]動[どう]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は車を運転するのが好きだ。
example_sentences.english: My older brother likes driving a car.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は車[くるま]を運[うん]転[てん]するのが好[す]きだ。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と一緒に荷物を運んだ。
example_sentences.english: I carried the luggage together with my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に荷[に]物[もつ]を運[はこ]んだ。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A mound of <radical>earth</radical> sits on top, underneath a sealed <radical>cocoon</radical> tucked out of sight. Whatever was inside wrapped up and went under the soil. Dig the mound over: nothing is left. It is <kanji>gone</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kyo is the magician who buries things and cannot get them back. He taps the mound, says 「<reading>きょ</reading>」 with a flourish, and that is genuinely the end of the trick. No reappearance, no second half. きょ, and it is gone.

items.mnemonic_text: Legs launching outward from a bow: departure, emitting.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Off the blocks, the <radical>outspread legs</radical> explode sideways. The racer's <radical>human legs</radical> land planted wide just as <radical>two</radical> chopsticks clatter off a dropped bento — chasing a train already <kanji>departed</kanji>, hissing steam as it pulls away without them.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the platform, a conductor named <reading>Hatsu</reading> slams the doors and yells <reading>はつ</reading> into his whistle as steam bursts from the wheels — one word, and the train is already gone.

example_sentences.japanese: これは新しい発明です。
example_sentences.english: This is a new invention.
example_sentences.furigana: これは新[あたら]しい発[はつ]明[めい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はその発明が好きです。
example_sentences.english: He likes that invention.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はその発[はつ]明[めい]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: その発明はとても便利です。
example_sentences.english: That invention is very convenient.
example_sentences.furigana: その発[はつ]明[めい]はとても便[べん]利[り]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A stylized heart shape with three drips of feeling.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You find the cartoon <radical>heart</radical> on Grandma Kane's mossy steps, left lobe puffed, cleft pinched, point tapping the moss. Shrine cats bat the three leftover beats bouncing in the chambers, and it cannot hold one quiet thought. That jitter is a <kanji>heart</kanji> and a mind, still mid-thump.
items.reading_mnemonic: You watch Shinny jog up the mossy steps in sandals too big. He misses the bell rope and plants his <reading>shin</reading> on the bronze rim instead, then folds onto the moss groaning <reading>しん</reading> as the leftover beats bounce once for each groan.
items.description: 心 is the cartoon heart: left lobe, cleft, point, and three bouncing beats. 必 is that same heart with one extra diagonal stroke slashing through it.

example_sentences.japanese: 母はいつも私のことを心配する。
example_sentences.english: My mother always worries about me.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]はいつも私[わたし]のことを心[しん]配[ぱい]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はとても熱心な先生です。
example_sentences.english: She is a very enthusiastic teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はとても熱[ねっ]心[しん]な先[せん]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は試験のことを心配していた。
example_sentences.english: My little sister was worried about the exam.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は試[し]験[けん]のことを心[しん]配[ぱい]していた。

items.mnemonic_text: An old man's (耂) bent posture, deep in thought.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the crosswalk, that stooped, unhurried <radical>old</radical> man stops dead in the middle, one hand cupped like the lopsided <radical>wrap</radical> that never quite fits the watermelon. Except now it's cupped around his own chin. Traffic idles as he turns something over, wrapping his mind around a problem before moving. That's <kanji>thinking</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, spots the old man frozen mid-crosswalk and can't restock the onigiri shelf until he moves. A crow on the awning tips its head and <reading>caws</reading> — <reading>こう</reading> — the exact sound of someone thinking too hard to hurry.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は質問を考えました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher thought about the question.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は質[しつ]問[もん]を考[かんが]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は宿題の答えを考えています。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother is thinking about the homework answer.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]の答[こた]えを考[かんが]えています。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は新しい料理を考え出しました。
example_sentences.english: She came up with a new dish.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は新[あたら]しい料[りょう]理[り]を考え出[かんがえだ]しました。

items.mnemonic_text: A tree (木) crossed with mingling students: a school.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tree</radical> stands in the courtyard, one wide branch spread over the whole yard. Your <radical>father</radical> has dragged the barbecue out under it, tongs held high, announcing lunch to four hundred kids at once. He snaps the pot <radical>lid</radical> down over the grill so the smoke doesn't trip the hallway alarm. Bells, homework, and dad grilling under the tree — this is <kanji>school</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, has set up a pop-up shop right inside the school gate, restocking onigiri between classes and muttering <reading>こう</reading>, こう as he lines up the shelves. The kids buy their lunch from him before the bell.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 校庭に犬がいます。

example_sentences.furigana: 校[こう]庭[てい]に犬[いぬ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、学校を休みます。
example_sentences.english: I will take a day off from school today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、学[がっ]校[こう]を休[やす]みます。

items.mnemonic_text: A tall tower with windows: high and expensive.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tall</radical> tower with windows standing over the town — but notice the open <radical>mouth</radical> at its base, an entrance yawning wide for anyone brave enough to climb. It's the fanciest, most expensive building around, and everyone cranes their neck to see how <kanji>tall</kanji> it is.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, is jealous of that tall tower, so he stacks his onigiri shelves higher and higher until they're the tallest — and priciest — display in town. As the tower of rice balls wobbles, he shouts <reading>こう</reading> to warn a customer before it topples.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、高い時計を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought an expensive watch yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、高[たか]い時計[とけい]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの山は高いです。
example_sentences.english: That mountain over there is tall.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: あのレストランの肉は高いです。
example_sentences.english: The meat at that restaurant is expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: あのレストランの肉[にく]は高[たか]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) wound to its winter (冬) finish: to end.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sits on the shrine steps unspooling a length of <radical>thread</radical>. Tied to the very end is a duckling towed along by its <radical>trailing foot</radical>, webbed foot skidding on the mossy stone. The spool runs out, the duckling skids to a stop at her feet, and there is nowhere left to go — that's the <kanji>end</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The instant the thread runs out, one of the shrine cats pounces on the duckling's lace. It clamps its teeth down like it's stealing a <reading>shoe</reading>. Its triumphant yowl comes out as <reading>しゅう</reading> — the exact sound of the last stretch of thread giving way.

example_sentences.japanese: 宿題はもう終わりました。
example_sentences.english: I already finished my homework.
example_sentences.furigana: 宿[しゅく]題[だい]はもう終[お]わりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 映画の終わりはとても悲しいです。
example_sentences.english: The end of the movie is very sad.
example_sentences.furigana: 映[えい]画[が]の終[お]わりはとても悲[かな]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨はもうすぐ終わります。
example_sentences.english: The rain will be over soon.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]はもうすぐ終[お]わります。

items.mnemonic_text: Bad luck (歹) beside a person collapsed: to die.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon is still airborne, gripping the bent <radical>spoon</radical> from that leveraged scoop of ice cream, and comes down hard on the already-cracked corner of <radical>death / bad luck</radical>. The bone gives way under the impact, nothing left to set or straighten. That's the whole story: <kanji>die</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the register at Koichi's konbini, the cashier named <reading>She</reading> hears the crash and doesn't even look up, just breathes one flat <reading>し</reading> and rings up the shattered tub anyway. Nothing about tonight is going to surprise her.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、猫が死にました。
example_sentences.english: The cat died yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、猫[ねこ]が死[し]にました。

example_sentences.japanese: この魚はもう死んでいます。
example_sentences.english: This fish is already dead.
example_sentences.furigana: この魚[さかな]はもう死[し]んでいます。

example_sentences.japanese: この木は冬に死にました。
example_sentences.english: This tree died in the winter.
example_sentences.furigana: この木[き]は冬[ふゆ]に死[し]にました。

items.mnemonic_text: Words (言) given a式 (form/ceremony): a formal test.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the ceremony marking a new <radical>construction</radical> site, someone hammers the flagged <radical>stake</radical> into the dirt. They clear their throat and give it a go — a shaky <radical>speech</radical>, words bubbling out one line at a time, nobody rehearsed. Stake planted, speech barely holding together: that shaky first attempt is the very definition of <kanji>a try</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A foreman named <reading>Shii</reading> paces around the ceremony, hissing a stressed <reading>し</reading> through his teeth every time the speech wobbles. He's sure the whole shaky test is about to collapse before the stake settles into the ground.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、日本語の試験を受けます。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'm taking a Japanese exam.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、日本[にほん]語[ご]の試[し]験[けん]を受[う]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今週は試験があります。
example_sentences.english: There's an exam this week.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[こん]週[しゅう]は試[し]験[けん]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 試験は難しかったです。
example_sentences.english: The exam was difficult.
example_sentences.furigana: 試[し]験[けん]は難[むずか]しかったです。

items.mnemonic_text: A standing tree cut by an axe (斤): freshly new.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>spicy</radical> man hauls his pepper skewer into the showroom, eyes streaming. He swears the sauce is mild. Behind him stands a <radical>tree</radical>, roots and all — an <radical>axe</radical> felled it just this morning, sap still wet. An attendant <radical>standing</radical> beside it throws out both arms so nobody touches it. Just cut, just felled, just unwrapped: everything here is <kanji>new</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The showroom greeter is Shin, and every time a new model rolls in he shouts his own name — <reading>しん</reading>! — as he yanks the cover off. Whatever Shin unveils is always brand new.
items.description: Means "new"; a very common kanji appearing in words for new things, newspapers, and freshness.

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい車を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new car.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい車[くるま]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 父は毎朝新聞を読みます。
example_sentences.english: My father reads the newspaper every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]新[しん]聞[ぶん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: あの新しいレストランはおいしいです。
example_sentences.english: That new restaurant is delicious.
example_sentences.furigana: あの新[あたら]しいレストランはおいしいです。

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth releasing lines of speech: to say.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the bottom of this character and you'll find a <radical>mouth</radical>, wide open. Above it, stacked up in neat horizontal lines, is everything that mouth is pushing out — layer after layer of <radical>speech</radical>. A mouth releasing stacked lines like that is exactly what it means to say a <kanji>word</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a general in full armor climbs the mossy steps and won't stop giving orders — every word out of his mouth is a barked command. The cats scatter as the general says "<reading>げん</reading>!" like it's the only word he knows.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は何と言いましたか。
example_sentences.english: What did the teacher say?
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は何[なに]と言[い]いましたか。

example_sentences.japanese: この言葉の意味が分かりません。
example_sentences.english: I don't understand the meaning of this word.
example_sentences.furigana: この言[こと]葉[ば]の意[い]味[み]が分[わ]かりません。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は面白いことを言います。
example_sentences.english: He says interesting things.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は面[おも]白[しろ]いことを言[い]います。

items.mnemonic_text: Feet advancing (辶) among matched (巽) options: to choose.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail is the same winding <radical>road</radical> you've been climbing, footsteps advancing toward the summit — except today it forks three ways around the vending machine. You plant one foot on a fork and commit, ignoring the other two. Deciding which path to advance down is what it means to <kanji>choose</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At that same fork, a hiker named <reading>Sen</reading> freezes completely, muttering <reading>せん</reading> over and over while staring at the vending machine, unable to advance a single step until he finally commits to a path.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はケーキを選びました。
example_sentences.english: She chose a cake.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はケーキを選[えら]びました。

example_sentences.japanese: どの色を選びますか。
example_sentences.english: Which color will you choose?
example_sentences.furigana: どの色[いろ]を選[えら]びますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は静かな部屋を選びました。
example_sentences.english: I chose a quiet room.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は静[しず]かな部屋[へや]を選[えら]びました。

items.mnemonic_text: A lamp's flame steady atop its stand: the main, central one.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Three flat <radical>king / jewel</radical> crowns wobble, skewered by one iron spike. Just as the pile threatens to slide off, a single <radical>drop</radical> of wax falls from the chandelier and seals the topmost crown in place. That fused stack is the one everyone bows to — the <kanji>main</kanji> one, the lord of the room.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back on the throne, the king's valet holds up the lord's one remaining polished <reading>shoe</reading> and announces <reading>しゅ</reading> to the court. The shoe proves who's still the main one in charge, wax-sealed crown and all.
items.description: 主 differs from 王 by exactly one mark: 主 adds a small drop stroke sitting above the top horizontal line, before the three stacked bars begin, while 王 has no dot at all — just the three flat crowns and the single spike through the middle, nothing above the topmost bar.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の姉のご主人は先生です。
example_sentences.english: My older sister's husband is a teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の姉[あね]のご主[しゅ]人[じん]は先[せん]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: あの女の人は主婦です。
example_sentences.english: That woman is a housewife.
example_sentences.furigana: あの女[おんな]の人[ひと]は主[しゅ]婦[ふ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女のご主人はいつも忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: Her husband is always busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]のご主[しゅ]人[じん]はいつも忙[いそが]しいです。

items.mnemonic_text: Power (力) worked in the rice field (田): a working man.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>rice field</radical> stretching out under the sun, and the one person out there doing the heavy lifting. He bends his arm, flexes his <radical>power</radical>, and drags the plow across the paddies all day. Someone with that much power working the rice field — that's the <kanji>man</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The man out in the field takes a break and starts pounding out a rhythm on his empty water bucket: <reading>だん</reading>, だん, だん. Every man on the trail can hear that drumbeat and grins.

example_sentences.japanese: あの男の人は誰ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is that man over there?
example_sentences.furigana: あの男[おとこ]の人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 小さい男の子が犬を見ました。
example_sentences.english: A small boy saw a dog.
example_sentences.furigana: 小[ちい]さい男[おとこ]の子[こ]が犬[いぬ]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 男の人が部屋に入りました。
example_sentences.english: A man entered the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 男[おとこ]の人[ひと]が部屋[へや]に入[はい]りました。

items.mnemonic_text: Words (言) matched all around (周): to check, investigate.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till keeps beeping over a missing onigiri. The manager lines up three suspects and cups his ear at each one in turn. Every time a mouth opens, another stack of horizontal <radical>speech</radical> bubbles rises off it, alibi after alibi piling until one stack cracks and the truth spills out. <kanji>Investigate</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the register stands a beat cop named Chow, notebook open, tallying every stacked bubble. He grunts <reading>ちょう</reading>, <reading>Chow</reading>, each time a suspect's story shifts, until his tally points straight at the onigiri thief hiding behind the till.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は学生の意見を調査した。
example_sentences.english: The teacher looked into the students' opinions.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は学[がく]生[せい]の意[い]見[けん]を調[ちょう]査[さ]した。

example_sentences.japanese: 警官はその問題の原因を調査している。
example_sentences.english: The police officer is investigating the cause of that problem.
example_sentences.furigana: 警[けい]官[かん]はその問[もん]題[だい]の原[げん]因[いん]を調[ちょう]査[さ]している。

example_sentences.japanese: 会社は新しい市場を調査した。
example_sentences.english: The company looked into a new market.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]は新[あたら]しい市[し]場[じょう]を調[ちょう]査[さ]した。

items.mnemonic_text: A cross pushed into the ground: earth and soil.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a simple cross being pushed straight down into the <radical>earth</radical>, staking out a plot of dirt. The moment its base sinks in, the loose brown stuff piles up around it. That cross pressed into the ground is <kanji>earth</kanji>, plain soil.
items.reading_mnemonic: A gardener drops to his knees in the plot and starts digging with his bare hands, going "do, do, do" (<reading>ど</reading>) as he flings soil over his shoulder. Every heavy handful he tosses out lands with that same low ど grunt.

example_sentences.japanese: 土曜日に公園へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to the park on Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎週土曜日に海へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the sea every Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]週[しゅう]土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]に海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今週の土曜日は忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: I am busy this Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[こん]週[しゅう]の土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]は忙[いそが]しいです。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) tangled in a tree (木): sunrise in the east.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>sun</radical> rising and getting tangled in the branches of a <radical>tree</radical> on the horizon. You see the sun caught right behind that tree first thing in the morning — and the sun always comes up in the east. Sun plus tree, hung together at dawn: that's <kanji>east</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker faces the sunrise and lets out a long, tired yawn — a huge "<reading>とう</reading>" that echoes down the slope. Every morning she climbs to greet the east with that same sleepy とう.

example_sentences.japanese: 東の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I open the east window.
example_sentences.furigana: 東[ひがし]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の東で友達に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met a friend east of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の東[ひがし]で友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの町は東です。
example_sentences.english: That town is to the east.
example_sentences.furigana: あの町[まち]は東[ひがし]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A box repeating the same shape inside: the same.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A wide box drops onto the level <radical>ground</radical> right outside Koichi's konbini, three walls up and no floor, blocking the door. You crouch down to peer through its open front — that's exactly the <radical>wide box</radical> you know. Staring back out of the gloom is a <radical>mouth</radical>, yawning out the very order you were about to say yourself. Same ground, same box, same mouth: <kanji>same</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, the mouth belongs to the onigiri baker, elbow-deep in <reading>dough</reading> behind the counter. Every time you ask what's going on, he just grunts <reading>どう</reading> without looking up — same shrug, same word, same batch of dough, every single time you ask.

example_sentences.japanese: これとそれは同じです。
example_sentences.english: This one and that one are the same.
example_sentences.furigana: これとそれは同[おな]じです。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは同じ会社で働いています。
example_sentences.english: We work at the same company.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは同[おな]じ会[かい]社[しゃ]で働[はたら]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕の傘は君のと同じ色だ。
example_sentences.english: My umbrella is the same color as yours.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]の傘[かさ]は君[きみ]のと同[おな]じ色[いろ]だ。

items.mnemonic_text: A heart (心) pierced by a single resolved stroke: certainly necessary.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>heart</radical> is still hooked low and flinging its three drops of blood when a cleaver comes down and pins it flat to the altar with one diagonal slash through the middle. A heart nailed down like that isn't optional anymore, it's simply <kanji>necessary</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine boy who nailed it down mutters a chant over the pinned heart, tapping the blade's handle twice for luck. It comes out as a flat little <reading>ひつ</reading> — like he's clearing his throat, <reading>hit-soo</reading> — before he can walk away.
items.description: 必 is 心 (heart) with one extra diagonal stroke slashing down across the hook from upper left to lower right. Without that slash, the three loose drops sit under a bare fishhook — that plain shape is 心 on its own. With it, the stroke pins straight through the hook, and that pinned, slashed heart is 必.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝必ずコーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I drink coffee every morning without fail.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]必[かなら]ずコーヒーを飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は約束の時間に必ず来ます。
example_sentences.english: He always comes at the promised time.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は約[やく]束[そく]の時[じ]間[かん]に必[かなら]ず来[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は宿題を必ず持って来ます。
example_sentences.english: I'll definitely bring my homework tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]を必[かなら]ず持[も]って来[き]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) under a covering (覀): the essential point, needed.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The talent show can't start without her: the <radical>woman</radical> frozen mid-dance, one leg swung wide and arms flung, is the only act the whole gym is waiting on. Every other performer gets cut from the lineup before her, because without that one dancer nothing here is <kanji>important</kanji> enough to keep.
items.reading_mnemonic: Backstage, the stage manager keeps checking his clipboard and groaning <reading>よう</reading>, the same sound he'd make chasing a lost <reading>yo-yo</reading> under the bleachers. The dancer still hasn't shown up, and the whole show needs her.

example_sentences.japanese: 傘が要りますか。
example_sentences.english: Do you need an umbrella?
example_sentences.furigana: 傘[かさ]が要[い]りますか。

example_sentences.japanese: これは重要な話です。
example_sentences.english: This is an important matter.
example_sentences.furigana: これは重[じゅう]要[よう]な話[はなし]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 今、お金が要ります。
example_sentences.english: I need money right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]、お金[かね]が要[い]ります。

items.mnemonic_text: A neck (首) moving down a path: the road and the way.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The giraffe in the business suit is late, so it lowers its long <radical>neck</radical> flat to the ground. The winding <radical>road</radical> unrolls straight along the top of it, spots and all. Commuters just walk up the giraffe and keep going. By lunchtime, nobody can tell where the animal ends and the way forward begins. This kanji is <kanji>road</kanji>, the way.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the road you meet a doe standing in the middle of the path, blocking the way. She won't budge, so you call out "<reading>どう</reading> do I get past you?" — and the doe just chews and stares, owning the whole road.
items.description: Means road or way; a very common kanji seen in words for streets, paths, and figurative "ways" of doing things.

example_sentences.japanese: この道は長いです。
example_sentences.english: This road is long.
example_sentences.furigana: この道[みち]は長[なが]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日道を歩きます。
example_sentences.english: I walk along the road every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]道[みち]を歩[ある]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 道の近くに公園があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a park near the road.
example_sentences.furigana: 道[みち]の近[ちか]くに公[こう]園[えん]があります。

items.mnemonic_text: Two people back to back turning away from the cold north.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon has landed in a snowdrift, still gripping the bent <radical>spoon</radical> it levered out of the ice cream tub. It sits back-to-back with a second raccoon on a frozen bench, both hunched away from the gale. The <radical>spoon</radical> is frozen solid to its paws. That wind is coming straight down from the <kanji>north</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, the wind off the northern peak is so brutal that a hiker named Hoku pulls his hood tight and mutters "<reading>ほく</reading>, ほく" through chattering teeth as he trudges. Hear him — ほく — every time you point north.

example_sentences.japanese: 北は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It is cold in the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 北から来ました。
example_sentences.english: I came from the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]から来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 北の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I will open the north window.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

items.mnemonic_text: A person standing on the ground line: to stand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person planted firmly on the ground, feet apart, refusing to budge — they <radical>stand</radical> there, solid and upright. That single image, a person rooted on the earth, is the whole character: to <kanji>stand</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A soldier named Ritsu snaps to attention on the mountain trail, standing so straight you could measure a wall against him. Every time someone shouts "<reading>りつ</reading>!" he stands up even taller.
items.description: Means "stand"; a common N5 kanji appearing in words about standing up, standing something upright, and establishing or setting things in place.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生はドアの前に立っています。
example_sentences.english: The teacher is standing in front of the door.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]はドアの前[まえ]に立[た]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は立って、窓を開けました。
example_sentences.english: I stood up and opened the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は立[た]って、窓[まど]を開[あ]けました。

example_sentences.japanese: あそこに男の人が立っています。
example_sentences.english: A man is standing over there.
example_sentences.furigana: あそこに男[おとこ]の人[ひと]が立[た]っています。

items.mnemonic_text: A person (亻) in motion (動): working.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> hauls up the mountain trail before dawn, a <radical>power</radical>-flexed arm dragging them past the vending machine. The <radical>sun</radical> crawls across the sky while both boots grind toward solid <radical>ground</radical> at the summit — still not done. That sunrise-to-sunset climb is <kanji>work</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the very top, a badger named <reading>Dobu</reading> slumps against that same vending machine and groans <reading>どう</reading> into the empty air. It isn't a question — the sound of a body that has decided the climb was too much work.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は銀行で働きます。
example_sentences.english: I work at a bank.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は銀[ぎん]行[こう]で働[はたら]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は病院で働いています。
example_sentences.english: She's working at the hospital.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は病[びょう]院[いん]で働[はたら]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 父は毎日忙しく働きます。
example_sentences.english: My father works hard every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は毎[まい]日[にち]忙[いそが]しく働[はたら]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A person with sparks flying off each side: fire.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person standing with their arms flung out, and sparks are flying off them in every direction. They're crackling, glowing, throwing off heat — this is a person who has become <radical>fire</radical>. Every time you see 火, see that sparking figure and think: <kanji>fire</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and lets out a puff of flame with a raspy caw: 「<reading>か</reading>!」. The flame and the sound arrive together, so when you see this fire kanji, you hear Kaa's か.

example_sentences.japanese: 火曜日に友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: On Tuesday I'm watching a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週の火曜日はとても忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: Next Tuesday I'm really busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]の火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]はとても忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 火曜日の朝、公園に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Tuesday morning, I'm going to the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]の朝[あさ]、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: Bamboo (竹) matching (合) the right response: an answer.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two stalks of <radical>bamboo</radical> in Sei's schoolyard lean together, leaves flicking. Right between their roots the level <radical>ground</radical> splits along one flat crack. A wide square <radical>mouth</radical> yawns up out of the gap — not to ask anything, just to blurt out the <kanji>answer</kanji> before you've finished asking.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei stubs her toe on the bamboo root right where the ground cracked open, and yelps instead of answering the teacher's question. Everyone laughs, but the barked <reading>とう</reading> still counts — a stubbed <reading>toe</reading> makes exactly that sound, and gets treated as her answer anyway.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は先生の質問に答えました。
example_sentences.english: I answered the teacher's question.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は先[せん]生[せい]の質[しつ]問[もん]に答[こた]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: その問題の答えが分かりません。
example_sentences.english: I don't know the answer to that problem.
example_sentences.furigana: その問[もん]題[だい]の答[こた]えが分[わ]かりません。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は質問にすぐ答えました。
example_sentences.english: She answered the question right away.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は質[しつ]問[もん]にすぐ答[こた]えました。

items.mnemonic_text: A bird settling into its nest as the sun sets in the west.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a squat bird cage with a little bird perched inside, its legs dangling below the frame. At sunset the birds all fly home to roost, settling in the cage as the sun sinks in the same direction. That cage where everything comes to rest for the night points you toward the <kanji>west</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, insists she always knows exactly where the sun sets. She marches to the western edge of the sports field at dusk and points. She calls out 「<reading>せい</reading>, that way!」 while the whole class watches the sky turn orange behind her.
items.description: 西 and 四 are both boxes with strokes inside. 四 is a plain rectangle with two short legs bending inward. 西 sits an extra horizontal bar across the very top, above the box, which 四 never has.

example_sentences.japanese: 学校は町の西です。
example_sentences.english: The school is in the west of the town.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]は町[まち]の西[にし]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は西から来ました。
example_sentences.english: He came from the west.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は西[にし]から来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは一緒に西へ行きました。
example_sentences.english: We went west together.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは一[いっ]緒[しょ]に西[にし]へ行[い]きました。

items.mnemonic_text: A foot planted firmly: stop.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You're mid-stride down the mountain trail when you plant one foot flat and hard against the ground and <radical>stop</radical> in place. That single planted foot is the whole picture: it's rooted, going nowhere. A planted foot means <kanji>stop</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Right where you stopped, you hear a sharp "<reading>し</reading>!" — someone shushing you. It's the vending machine at the top of the trail, hissing "し, し" as it refuses to dispense until you stop and wait. That shushing し is the sound to hold onto.
items.description: Means "stop" and is the base of common verbs like 止まる and 止める, showing up anywhere something halts or is brought to a halt.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の前にバスが止まりました。
example_sentences.english: The bus stopped in front of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の前[まえ]にバスが止[と]まりました。

example_sentences.japanese: ここでタクシーを止めてください。
example_sentences.english: Please stop the taxi here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここでタクシーを止[と]めてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 古い時計が止まりました。
example_sentences.english: The old clock stopped.
example_sentences.furigana: 古[ふる]い時計[とけい]が止[と]まりました。

items.mnemonic_text: Grasping (⺈) at the heart (心): an urgent hurry.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>broom</radical>'s cat sleeps through it, so crumbs and cat skid down the hallway fast. Someone chasing it yanks the <radical>wrap</radical> around the watermelon, and the jolt sets the <radical>heart</radical> — hook flicking, three drops flung loose — pounding in a panicked sprint. Everyone is in a <kanji>hurry</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Skidding into that same hallway, a courier pigeon named <reading>Cue</reading> can't stop in time and slams into the pile, wheezing out a strangled <reading>きゅう</reading> as crumbs and feathers go flying. He's always this late, and it's always this loud.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅まで急いでください。
example_sentences.english: Please hurry to the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]まで急[いそ]いでください。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨が降る前に、家へ急ぎましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's hurry home before it rains.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]る前[まえ]に、家[いえ]へ急[いそ]ぎましょう。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝、学校へ急いで行きました。
example_sentences.english: In the morning, I hurried to school.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]、学[がっ]校[こう]へ急[いそ]いで行[い]きました。

items.mnemonic_text: A shelter (广) opening onto open ground: wide, spacious.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That cliffside <radical>shelter</radical> turns out to be absurdly wide — its diagonal roof floats over so much open air that a whole field fits underneath. A silkworm tries to seal itself into a <radical>cocoon</radical> in one corner, spinning the closing loop again and again, but the space is too wide for it to ever meet the other edge. <kanji>Wide</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi surveys his newly renovated konbini — the fluorescent aisles now stretch so wide he needs a golf cart to reach the onigiri shelf. He beams at the beeping till and announces, <reading>こう</reading>, this is what real square footage feels like, pure <reading>Koh</reading>-style efficiency at last.

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は広いです。
example_sentences.english: This room is spacious.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は広[ひろ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の家はあまり広くないです。
example_sentences.english: My house isn't very big.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の家[いえ]はあまり広[ひろ]くないです。

example_sentences.japanese: その公園はとても広いです。
example_sentences.english: That park is very spacious.
example_sentences.furigana: その公[こう]園[えん]はとても広[ひろ]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Two people (人) sitting on the earth (土) under a roof.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two of those striding <radical>person</radical> figures come in from the cold. They duck under the lean-to <radical>shelter</radical> nailed into the rock face, out of the rain at last. They drop straight down onto the same patch of <radical>earth</radical> underneath it, shoulder to shoulder. They flatly refuse to get up again. Two walkers on the ground under a roof want exactly one thing: to <kanji>sit</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The person who settles onto that patch of earth is Zara, and the moment she sits she lets out a long, satisfied "<reading>ざ</reading>あ" of relief. Every time you see someone plop down here, you hear Zara's ざ.
items.description: Means "sit"; shows up in words about sitting down, seats, and taking a seat.

example_sentences.japanese: 誰がここに座りましたか。
example_sentences.english: Who sat here?
example_sentences.furigana: 誰[だれ]がここに座[すわ]りましたか。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が机の下に座っています。
example_sentences.english: The cat is sitting under the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が机[つくえ]の下[した]に座[すわ]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達の隣に座りました。
example_sentences.english: I sat next to my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]の隣[となり]に座[すわ]りました。

items.mnemonic_text: A person (亻) directing an official (吏): to use, to employ.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a <radical>person</radical> plants both feet on one patch of <radical>ground</radical>. They fling their <radical>mouth</radical> wide, bellowing orders at everyone scrubbing laundry — never lifting a hand, just pointing. That bossy, hands-off stance is <kanji>use</kanji>: someone else's effort put to work on your command.
items.reading_mnemonic: Shiba the heron struts along that same riverbank, screeching orders of his own at the laundry crew like a tiny drill sergeant. The sound comes out as a piercing <reading>し</reading>, pure <reading>sheesh</reading>, every single time someone slacks off scrubbing.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日パソコンを使います。
example_sentences.english: I use my computer every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]パソコンを使[つか]います。

example_sentences.japanese: このペンはまだ使えます。
example_sentences.english: This pen still works.
example_sentences.furigana: このペンはまだ使[つか]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はこの部屋を使いました。
example_sentences.english: He used this room.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はこの部屋[へや]を使[つか]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: Rice (米) measured with a dipper (斗): materials, a fee.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the baker plunges the trusted <radical>dipper</radical> into a sack of <radical>rice</radical>, its grains scattering as it comes up loaded and level. He tips it into a paper bag, marks a tally on the register, and charges by the scoop — the material measured out becomes exactly the <kanji>fee</kanji> you pay.
items.reading_mnemonic: A customer named <reading>Leo</reading> counts each dipper-load of rice as it clinks into his bag, muttering <reading>りょう</reading>, <reading>りょう</reading>. He keeps track of how many scoops he owes, until his tally and the register's total match up, scoop for scoop.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日料理します。
example_sentences.english: I cook every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]料[りょう]理[り]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は料理が上手です。
example_sentences.english: She's good at cooking.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は料[りょう]理[り]が上手[じょうず]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 給料で新しい靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought new shoes with my salary.
example_sentences.furigana: 給[きゅう]料[りょう]で新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A bird (隹) landing on a tree (木) with the flock: to gather.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Word gets out on the pigeon grapevine, and by dusk every <radical>old bird</radical> in town has shuffled onto the same <radical>tree</radical>. Too stiff to fly, they hop branch to branch. Soon the whole trunk is buried under birds who refuse to leave. The tree has <kanji>gathered</kanji> every last one of them.
items.reading_mnemonic: Up in the branches, an arborist swats at the crowd of old birds and yells <reading>Shoo</reading>, <reading>しゅう</reading>. Not one bird moves off the tree — there are too many, and shooing just isn't going to cut it today.

items.mnemonic_text: A warm shelter facing the sunny south.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody upends a <radical>wide box</radical> on the hot sand. Across its flat top, two matchsticks lie laid in a <radical>cross</radical>, like the world's worst weather vane. A flamingo nudges the box round and round all afternoon. Whichever arm ends up warmest — that one points <kanji>south</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A backpacker named Nan has been hiking down the mountain trail for days, always heading south toward warmer weather. Every time someone asks which way she's going, she just points and sighs, "<reading>なん</reading>... south, always south." The word なん sticks because Nan won't stop saying it.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の南は海です。
example_sentences.english: South of the station is the sea.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の南[みなみ]は海[うみ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は南の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I will open the south window.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は南[みなみ]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は南から来ました。
example_sentences.english: He came from the south.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は南[みなみ]から来[き]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: Two people standing side by side: to compare.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Outside Koichi's konbini, two identical clerks stand shoulder to shoulder, backs flat, chins level, each daring the other to be an inch taller. Neither moves, neither blinks — they just stand there side by side under the fluorescent light, forever being <kanji>compared</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: One clerk finally cracks and jabs a thumb at himself, shouting <reading>ひ</reading> — insisting <reading>He</reading>'s obviously the taller one. The other clerk just narrows his eyes and keeps standing there under the konbini lights, refusing to concede an inch.
items.description: 比 almost never stands alone as a word. In everyday use it shows up bound into other kanji or attached as 比べる, and mostly in contexts about ratios and percentages rather than as a freestanding term by itself.

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth over stopping legs: a foot that carries you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> sits on top of a pair of legs. The legs have skidded to a halt — they are <radical>stopping</radical> hard. They end in one part: a <radical>foot</radical>. That's your <kanji>foot</kanji>, your leg, plenty to stand on.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named Sok is nursing a blister on her foot. Every painful step she counts out loud, 「<reading>そく</reading>、そく、そく」, until she finally reaches the vending machine at the top and decides that's enough walking for one day.
items.description: Means foot, leg, or to suffice/be enough; shows up in words for body parts and in verbs about having sufficient amounts.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は足が長いです。
example_sentences.english: She has long legs.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は足[あし]が長[なが]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 足が冷たいです。
example_sentences.english: My feet are cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 足[あし]が冷[つめ]たいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬は足が速いです。
example_sentences.english: Dogs run fast.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]は足[あし]が速[はや]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Standing (立) by a tree (木) watching (見): a parent's love.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the edge of Sei's school field, someone has climbed a <radical>tree</radical> and wedged themselves to <radical>stand</radical> on the highest branch. They crane forward to <radical>see</radical> every second of the match without missing a kick. That straining figure, who won't leave until it's over, is a <kanji>parent</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: When the final whistle blows, they scramble down too fast and bark their <reading>しん</reading> — their <reading>shin</reading> — hard against a branch, then limp off still cheering about the goal.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の親はいつも忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: My parent is always busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の親[おや]はいつも忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅員はとても親切でした。
example_sentences.english: The station staff was very kind.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]員[いん]はとても親[しん]切[せつ]でした。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼の親は先生です。
example_sentences.english: His parent is a teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]の親[おや]は先[せん]生[せい]です。

items.mnemonic_text: Feathers (羽) over white (白): a bird practicing to fly, to learn.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a duckling flings itself off a rock trying to fly. Each failed launch yanks loose a pair of stiff <radical>feather</radical> plumes drifting onto the water. It keeps aiming for one bead of milk on a lilypad, glinting <radical>white</radical> in the sun. Attempt after attempt, feathers scattering, glint out of reach — that relentless repeating is <kanji>learn and practice</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A birdwatcher named Shoe sits on the bank with a clipboard, tally marks climbing with every failed launch. She murmurs <reading>しゅう</reading>, <reading>Shoe</reading> under her breath at each attempt, certain the duckling will get airborne if it just keeps practicing.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は日本語を習いました。
example_sentences.english: I learned Japanese.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は日本[にほん]語[ご]を習[なら]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は毎日ピアノを練習します。
example_sentences.english: She practices piano every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は毎[まい]日[にち]ピアノを練[れん]習[しゅう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: これは私の習慣です。
example_sentences.english: This is a habit of mine.
example_sentences.furigana: これは私[わたし]の習[しゅう]慣[かん]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A tiny hook with two small dots: small.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single hook standing upright with two dots flanking it, one on each side, like something <radical>small</radical> pinched between two fingertips. It's so slight it could vanish if you sneezed. That tiny hook with its two little dots is the very picture of <kanji>small</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, snaps his white glove and shrinks the whole set until the doves look like specks. As everything gets impossibly small, the crowd gasps, "<reading>しょう</reading>!" — the man himself is the smallest thing on stage.
items.description: 小 is three strokes: a hooked vertical with a short dash on each side. 少 is 小 with a fourth stroke, a slash sweeping down to the left beneath it. If there is a tail, it is 少.

example_sentences.japanese: あの小さい猫を見ましたか。
example_sentences.english: Did you see that small cat?
example_sentences.furigana: あの小[ちい]さい猫[ねこ]を見[み]ましたか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の部屋は小さいです。
example_sentences.english: My room is small.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の部屋[へや]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、小さい本を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a small book yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、小[ちい]さい本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> on the left; on the right <radical>two</radical> bars over <radical>ground</radical>, each on a <radical>stick</radical>, <radical>split</radical> into legs at the foot. A tray, lifted with both hands for somebody above to take: to <kanji>submit</kanji> a thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kyou is the offering-bearer who never lowers the tray. He walks the entire length of the hall with it over his head, announcing himself at every pillar — 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — until somebody finally takes the weight off him.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) beside her child (子): a fondness, to like.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That bundled-up <radical>child</radical>, arms thrown wide, comes barreling down the konbini aisle and collides with the <radical>woman</radical>, one leg still crossed mid-step from catching her balance. She doesn't scold him — she wraps her flung-wide arms around him and holds on, delighted. That's what it looks like to <kanji>like</kanji> someone.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, watches from the till and tries to <reading>coax</reading> the toddler back with a sticker, murmuring <reading>こう</reading>, <reading>こう</reading>. But the kid's already found someone better to hug, so Koichi just restocks the onigiri instead.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は猫が好きです。
example_sentences.english: I like cats.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は猫[ねこ]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は魚が好きだ。
example_sentences.english: He likes fish.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は魚[さかな]が好[す]きだ。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の好きな飲み物はお茶です。
example_sentences.english: My favorite drink is tea.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の好[す]きな飲[の]み物[もの]はお茶[ちゃ]です。

items.mnemonic_text: Two axes (斤斤) weighing shells (貝) of value: quality, substance.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The woodsman's <radical>axe</radical> is still buried hilt-deep in the chopping block — that argument's over. A peddler crouches beside it and pries the <radical>money</radical> shell open until coins spill into his palm. He turns each one to the light, questioning it, weighing it, before he decides it has the <kanji>quality</kanji> worth the trade.
items.reading_mnemonic: The peddler pockets one more coin, but stump sawdust dusts his palm and it starts to itch. Sheesh, itchy, he hisses, shaking his hand out and blowing grit off the last coin, muttering <reading>しつ</reading>, <reading>しつ</reading> — the sound comes out exactly like his <reading>itchy</reading> complaint.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は質問があります。
example_sentences.english: I have a question.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は質[しつ]問[もん]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女に質問しました。
example_sentences.english: I asked her a question.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]に質[しつ]問[もん]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生が質問に答えました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher answered the question.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]が質[しつ]問[もん]に答[こた]えました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lid</radical> is pulled across the sky, and a <radical>person</radical> slips under as the last <radical>evening</radical> drains away. Once the lid is on, nothing more gets in: no sun, no colour. The lid down over the evening: <kanji>night</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ya is the yakitori man who only opens once the lid is down. The cart comes out of nowhere, the lantern goes up, and he calls one syllable into the dark — 「<reading>や</reading>」 — which is the entire advertisement. If you can hear や, it is night.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> climbs a <radical>road</radical>, its surface <radical>split</radical> into ruts of packed <radical>earth</radical>. The flock keeps stalling, but the last one clears the rise: the job is <kanji>accomplished</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Tatsu is the drover who marks the top of every hill the same way: one slap on the gatepost and a barked 「<reading>たつ</reading>」 — done, next. He has said it at every gate between here and the coast. たつ means it is finished.

items.mnemonic_text: A hand over a craftsman's tool, held in the left hand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A badger in a hard hat stands on the level <radical>ground</radical> of a <radical>construction</radical> site. A crane lowers a steel beam toward its slot. His right hand is busy holding a sandwich. So his other hand braces the swinging beam, taking the whole weight. That steadying hand is the hand on the <kanji>left</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A samurai marches into Koichi's konbini and slams down a coin with his left hand, barking "<reading>さ</reading>!" as he demands the last onigiri. Every time you see this kanji, hear that samurai's sharp さ ringing off the beeping till.
items.description: Means "left," the opposite of right; shows up constantly in directions and in the compound 左右 (left and right).

example_sentences.japanese: 駅は左です。
example_sentences.english: The station is on the left.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]は左[ひだり]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 左に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go left.
example_sentences.furigana: 左[ひだり]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 左の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I will open the left window.
example_sentences.furigana: 左[ひだり]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

items.mnemonic_text: A twisted shape over the heart (心): a bad feeling.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That same fishhook-shaped <radical>heart</radical>, flinging its three drops of blood from the barb, gets swallowed whole by a stray cat behind the shrine. It doesn't turn the cat mean — it just makes everything the cat does go wrong: knocked-over bins, hissing at nothing, one long streak of trouble. That's what a <kanji>bad</kanji> heart does.
items.reading_mnemonic: The cat, still hissing, gets its tail pinned under a fallen bin and yowls in pure <reading>awkward</reading> pain — <reading>あく</reading> — echoing off the shrine steps before it slinks away, guiltier than ever.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は天気が悪いです。
example_sentences.english: The weather is bad today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は天[てん]気[き]が悪[わる]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は目が悪いです。
example_sentences.english: He has poor eyesight.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は目[め]が悪[わる]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は気分が悪いです。
example_sentences.english: I feel sick.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は気[き]分[ぶん]が悪[わる]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Three peaks rising up: a mountain range.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the shape and count them: three peaks rising side by side, the middle one tallest, like a <radical>mountain</radical> range. You don't need a story here — the character is a picture. Those three peaks are a <kanji>mountain</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine has a face, and it greets every exhausted hiker like an old friend: "You made it — welcome, san (<reading>さん</reading>)!" It calls everyone さん because on this mountain, reaching the peak earns you respect.
items.description: Means "mountain"; a common N5 kanji seen in nature words and countless place and family names.

example_sentences.japanese: あの山は高いです。
example_sentences.english: That mountain is high.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末、友達と山に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the mountains with a friend on the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]、友[とも]達[だち]と山[やま]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 山の写真はどこですか。
example_sentences.english: Where is the photo of the mountain?
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]の写[しゃ]真[しん]はどこですか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tree</radical>: a <radical>stick</radical> straight up, branches <radical>split</radical> aside. A <radical>lid</radical> stroke lies atop, longer than the <radical>one</radical> below — the twig's last inch: the <kanji>end</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Matsu is the woodsman who only ever takes the tip. He climbs the whole tree, snips the last bud off the top of it, and calls down 「<reading>まつ</reading>」 to say he has got there. まつ means there is nothing above him.

items.mnemonic_text: A person (人) leaning on a tree (木): resting.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, you spot a <radical>person</radical> slumped sideways against a <radical>tree</radical>, leaning into the trunk like it's the comfiest chair in the world. A <radical>person</radical> plus the tree they're propped against — that's someone taking a well-earned <kanji>rest</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker leaning on that tree lets out a huge, happy sigh — "<reading>きゅう</reading>!" — the sound of every muscle finally letting go. Every time you picture that person melting into rest, you hear that きゅう escape.
items.description: Means "rest" and shows up in everyday words for taking breaks and days off, like 休み.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、仕事を休みます。
example_sentences.english: I will take a day off from work tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、仕[し]事[ごと]を休[やす]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: ここでちょっと休みましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's rest here for a bit.
example_sentences.furigana: ここでちょっと休[やす]みましょう。

example_sentences.japanese: 風邪で学校を休みました。
example_sentences.english: I took a day off from school because of a cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 風邪[かぜ]で学[がっ]校[こう]を休[やす]みました。
